analysis.one_liner: Lets mining companies occupy public land for roads, pipelines, and facilities without proving a mineral deposit exists.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 216-195 in May 2024, but the Senate Energy Committee never acted and it died when the term ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give holders of federal mining claims the right to use and occupy public land for mining-related construction — roads, transmission lines, pipelines, and support facilities — whether or not they have actually discovered a valuable mineral deposit on the land. It would also treat routine claim-maintenance fees as satisfying the legal requirement to pay fair market value for the use of public land. The House passed it on a near party-line vote; the Senate took no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Mining companies holding federal claims. They could build and maintain permanent infrastructure on public land without first proving a valuable mineral deposit exists, and paying annual claim fees would be deemed to meet the fair-market-value requirement for using public land — meaning the land would support mining roads, power lines, and pipelines at essentially no added cost to the companies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hardrock mining companies with federal claims

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives mining claimants a right to "use and occupy" public land to conduct operations "with or without the discovery of a valuable mineral deposit," covering prospecting through processing and reclamation.

The covered "operations" include "the construction and maintenance of any road, transmission line, pipeline, or any other necessary infrastructure or means of access on public land for a support facility" — whether or not that infrastructure sits on the mining claim itself.

A claimant who pays the required location and claim-maintenance fees "shall be deemed to satisfy" the Federal Land Policy and Management Act's requirement to pay fair market value to the United States for the use of public land.

The Congressional Research Service describes the bill as setting "a process to allow mine operations to use, occupy, and conduct operations" on public land regardless of whether a mineral deposit has been discovered.

analysis.who_pays: The public. Federal land management agencies would lose their main leverage point — requiring proof of a real discovery before allowing occupation — and taxpayers would forgo market value for land the government holds in trust. Recreation users, conservation interests, and communities near public land would face more permanent mining infrastructure on shared land.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that a claimant who pays routine location and claim-maintenance fees "shall be deemed to satisfy" the requirement under federal land law to pay fair market value to the United States for the use of public land — meaning the public would not receive market value for industrial use of its land.

The right to use and occupy public land would apply regardless of whether a valuable mineral deposit has been discovered, which could allow claim-holders to occupy land and build infrastructure on the strength of an unproven claim.

By removing the discovery requirement as a gate for ancillary occupation, the bill would make it harder for land managers to limit where mining-related roads, pipelines, and power lines are built across public land.

The bill's savings clause does preserve existing protections: it does not create rights on lands not open to mining, does not limit federal authority to regulate mining under the Endangered Species Act, the Wilderness Act, and other laws, and does not restore rights on lands already withdrawn from mining.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill answers a real problem: mining companies face legal uncertainty over whether they can use public land for roads and facilities tied to claims where no valuable mineral deposit has been formally proven. But it addresses that by removing the discovery requirement entirely and by declaring that small annual fees count as fair market value for industrial use of federal land. The public-land costs — forgone market value and reduced oversight of where mining infrastructure gets built — outweigh the certainty the industry gains. The savings clause limits the damage by leaving withdrawn lands and environmental laws untouched, but the core trade still favors the claim-holders.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 216-195 on May 8, 2024, was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the next day, and never received a vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Amodei introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, and it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.
The committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a 24-17 vote on February 6, 2024, and formally reported it on March 7, 2024.
On May 1, 2024, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez's motion to recommit — a motion to send the bill back to committee — was agreed to 210-204, with 204 Democrats in favor and only 6 Republicans.
House Republicans brought the bill back under a new rule (H. Res. 1194), and on May 8 the same motion to recommit failed 203-208, with 203 Democrats in favor and no Republicans.
The House passed the bill 216-195 on May 8, 2024: 207 of 217 voting Republicans in favor and 9 of 213 voting Democrats, versus 194 Democrats and 1 Republican opposed.
The Senate received the bill on May 9, 2024, and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The hardrock mining industry got a House victory but no new rights, because the Senate never acted and the bill expired. Public-land users and taxpayers kept the current rules, including the requirement that mining claims support a proven discovery before land can be occupied for infrastructure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public land kept the status quo; mining industry gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 207 of 217 voting Republicans in favor, only 9 of 213 voting Democrats, with 194 Democrats and 1 Republican opposed. The motion-to-recommit votes were even more lopsided, with 203-204 Democrats for and 0-6 Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would give claim-holders a statutory right to build and maintain roads, transmission lines, pipelines, and support facilities on public land without proving a valuable mineral deposit, and would treat routine claim fees as satisfying the fair-market-value requirement. The industry's gain comes at the public's expense: land held in trust would support industrial infrastructure at little cost to the companies.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and public-land conservation interests
industries.note: More permanent mining infrastructure — roads, power lines, pipelines — could be placed across public land with no discovery of a mineral deposit required, reducing land managers' ability to steer that infrastructure away from recreation and habitat areas. The savings clause preserves withdrawals and environmental laws, which limits but does not eliminate this cost.
